text:
The streetlights of Blackwood Bay flickered with an unnerving precision, each pulse synchronized in a way that felt wrong. David Vance leaned closer to the smudged photograph on his desk, the faint smell of iodine from the old newspaper clippings doing little to cut through the unusual clarity pressing in from outside. It wasn't just the absence of fog tonight; the air itself felt scrubbed clean, every distant sound – a dog’s bark, the groan of a buoy – unnaturally sharp, as if the town’s usual cacophony had been forced into a rigid, unsettling order.

A low hum vibrated through the floorboards, a sound less like a passing truck and more like the deep thrum of a forgotten engine beneath the earth. His coffee cup, still warm, rattled almost imperceptibly against its saucer. Outside, a strange, sulfurous mist had begun to curl from the storm drains, tracing pale, ghostly arteries along the wet asphalt. It wasn't thick, just pervasive, clinging to the lowest points, hinting at a hidden warmth beneath the cold, hard surface of Blackwood Bay. He ignored it, or tried to. This town had a way of manifesting its ailments, making the very ground beneath your feet feel like a fever dream.

David traced the faded ink on the photo: a local fisherman, missing now for three days, standing grim-faced beside a boat that looked too new, too clean for the bay. The enforced clarity of the night, the subterranean pulse, the rising mist—they felt less like random events and more like the town itself taking a deep, shuddering breath before a confession. He picked up his pen. Time to see what kind of truth bubbled up from the depths.
